sources.title: M&A in Medtech: The Boom in Portfolio Reshaping
key_facts: Medtech deal value rose year over year and rebounded above pre-2023 levels in 2025, bolstered by renewed strategic confidence and several large transactions.
Spin-offs and divestitures accounted for more than one-third of strategic deal value in the first 11 months of 2025, a noticeable increase from the previous five-year average.
The second half of 2025 nearly doubled first-half deal value as valuations continued to decline.

25% of companies pursuing a separation destroy a significant amount of shareholder value in the process.
Top-quartile companies that succeed in carve-outs substantially outperform by having a clear separation thesis and a sustainable roadmap to value creation.
Waters acquired BD's biosciences and diagnostics businesses as one of the large headline deals in 2025.
Stryker acquired Inari Medical as another large headline deal in 2025.
BD separated its biosciences and diagnostics solutions businesses to streamline its portfolio and accelerate performance in core markets.
Solventum divested its purification and filtration unit to support debt reduction and sharpen focus on core operations.
Medtronic and Johnson & Johnson announced activity signaling a broader shift toward portfolio focus and category leadership.
Robust dealmaking is expected to continue into 2026.
Softer valuations in 2026 will intensify competition for quality assets, making speed, conviction, and disciplined execution essential.

Serial, targeted, capability-building deals that sharpen a company's edge in robotics, diagnostics, or imaging can often be more effective in increasing category leadership than headline acquisitions.

sources.title: Future of medtech: Orchestrating the next evolution ...
key_facts: By 2035, medtech companies are poised to be defined not just by the devices they make, but by the ecosystems they enable.

Medtech companies are increasingly positioned to act as orchestrators of outcomes by connecting patients, providers, payers, pharma, technology partners, and others through data and intelligent systems.
Medtech is positioned at the intersection of diagnostics, devices, and data, uniquely equipped to design the infrastructure, standards, and governance that link technology to patient care.
Robotics, intelligent sensors, and agentic AI are expected to fundamentally change how patient care is delivered and how caregivers are enabled.
In hospitals, surgical robots integrate imaging and analytics to guide decisions in real time.
At home, AI-enabled systems support daily care, guiding patients safely and independently under virtual oversight and targeted caregiver interventions.
Healthcare generates an estimated 30 percent of the world's data, with a single hospital producing as much as 50 petabytes each year.
Up to 97 percent of healthcare data goes unused, and roughly 80 percent remains unstructured, limiting its value for clinical or operational decision-making.
Next-generation BCI and neuromodulation platforms convert brain or nerve activity into digital signals that guide continuous monitoring, adaptive therapy, and personalized rehabilitation.
Connected implants and wearable sensors capture movement and recovery data, linking patients, clinicians, and care teams to track outcomes and optimize rehabilitation in real time.
Cross-category integrations are connecting continuous glucose, sleep, and activity data to create comprehensive health profiles enabling both clinical oversight and patient self-management.
AI-enabled cardiac and pulmonary monitoring programs are reducing hospital readmissions for heart failure and COPD by detecting deterioration early and triggering proactive virtual interventions.
Continuous data from connected devices becomes the foundation of modern evidence generation, capturing safety, efficacy, and performance in real-world settings.
The medtech industry's next opportunity is to evolve from supplying devices to linking proven hospital strengths to the wider health ecosystem.
Success in medtech ecosystems will depend on shared governance, open standards, and ethical frameworks that ensure automation enhances rather than replaces human judgment.
market_data_points: Healthcare cost annual growth is approaching 8%.
The U.S. could face a shortfall of nearly 200,000 physicians by 2037.
A third of consumers report delaying or skipping needed care due to affordability.
Healthcare generates an estimated 30 percent of the world's data.
A single hospital produces as much as 50 petabytes of data each year.
Up to 97 percent of healthcare data goes unused.
Roughly 80 percent of healthcare data remains unstructured.

Next-generation devices and diagnostics will not only measure but interpret, communicate, and adapt.
Value-based reimbursement models are changing what it means to be 'innovative' in medtech.
Continuous glucose monitoring is being integrated with sleep and activity data to create comprehensive metabolic health profiles.
Brain-computer interfaces and neuromodulation platforms are emerging as connected systems for adaptive therapy and personalized rehabilitation.
Embedded sensing, ambient AI, integrated robotics, and connected workflows are converging as key hospital ecosystem dynamics.
Predictive tools are being used to manage patient flow, reduce complications, and shorten hospital length of stay.
The medtech industry is evolving from selling products to enabling systems across the care continuum.
regulatory_mentions: In 2025, U.S. and European authorities introduced guidance that expands the use of real-world data and adaptive artificial intelligence across the medical device lifecycle, from post-market monitoring to iterative improvement.
Regulatory frameworks in 2025 signal growing acceptance of continuous evidence generation, de-identified real-world data, and learning systems that evolve safely over time.
Regulation is struggling to keep pace with technology, creating pressure for medtech to help shape regulatory frameworks.
Public funding and value-based reimbursement models are changing reimbursement standards for medical innovation.
FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) standards are cited as enabling measurable gains in care coordination, safety, and patient outcomes when adopted.

sources.title: Next in medtech 2025: Prepare to win in the future of health

Profit pools in medtech are shifting toward product-enabled services, data-driven solutions, and integrated care models where value is created over time.
The home is becoming the hub for diagnosis, intervention, and recovery in the evolving healthcare model.
Hospitals are evolving into modular care ports designed for short-stay procedures.
Virtual teams, remote monitoring, and AI-supported decision-making are extending care far beyond traditional facilities.
Medtech companies are expected to evolve from stand-alone hardware to intelligent infrastructure.
Devices are described as moving beyond data collection to enabling real-time diagnostics and insights that guide decision-making across the care continuum.

Leaders in medtech are treating data as a product that is discoverable, consumable, and actively exchanged internally and through a robust data marketplace accessible to partners.

AI centers of excellence where business, technology, and clinical teams co-design, test, and launch solutions in rapid iterative sprints are identified as a proven accelerator for medtech operating model transformation.

Leading medtech companies are making deliberate choices about where to compete, where to partner, and how to share value through joint ventures, co-development partnerships, and collaborations with retailers, payers, or digital platforms.

sources.title: Pulse of the industry: Medical technology report 2021
key_facts: MedTech industry achieved record revenues of US$446 billion in 2020, growing for the fourth consecutive year at 6.3%.
MedTech revenue growth for the first half of 2021 was over 16%, demonstrating sector resiliency.
MedTech emerging leader companies (revenues below US$500 million) saw a 128% rise in valuations between January 2020 and August 2021.
MedTech valuations outperformed Pharma and Biotech by more than 50%.
R&D spending by pure-play MedTechs grew 17.2% to US$23.8 billion in 2020, the highest annual growth rate since before the 2007 financial crisis.
MedTech companies executed 288 M&A deals in the 12 months ending June 2021, the highest annual number since EY began tracking in 2007.
US and European VC investment in MedTech reached US$9.1 billion in the 12-month period to June 2021, up 34% over the previous year and the highest level in the past decade.
Total equity investment in MedTech reached a new peak of US$34 billion, comprising US$9 billion in VC, US$6 billion in IPO, US$4 billion in SPAC, and US$16 billion in follow-on investment.
The non-imaging-diagnostics segment recorded a 24% annual growth rate in 2020, largely from pandemic-related demand.
94% of commercial leaders and conglomerates that reported first-half 2021 financials improved their revenues compared to 2020.
Baxter signed a US$10.5 billion deal to acquire connected care specialist Hillrom in September 2021.
Philips purchased BioTelemetry, a maker of digital patient monitoring platforms and AI-based analytics, for US$2.8 billion.
Boston Scientific announced a US$1.3 billion buy-out of Preventice Solutions, which designs remote monitoring services and mobile health solutions for cardiac arrhythmia patients.
Siemens Healthineers acquired Varian Medical Systems for US$16.4 billion, the largest disclosed deal in the evaluated period.
The US Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services introduced the Acute Hospital Care At Home program, which had been adopted by 53 health systems and 116 hospitals across 29 states as of April 2021.

sources.title: 2026 Life sciences outlook | Deloitte Insights
key_facts: More than 75% of responding biopharma and medtech executives are confident in their own organizations' financial outlooks for 2026.
Only 41% of surveyed life sciences executives feel optimistic about the health of the global economy.
Surveyed medtech executives tend to be more optimistic about the future than their biopharma peers, with 81% anticipating revenue growth.
There is no statistically significant difference between the growth expectations of medtech executives in the United States (84%) and those in several countries outside the United States (78%).
Only 22% of life sciences leaders said they have successfully scaled AI, and just 9% reported achieving significant returns on these AI efforts.
One-third of respondents (33%) said connected care delivery is a top trend for 2026, a rise of 15 percentage points year over year.
35% of respondents cited customer adoption of digital tools as a top trend for 2026.
Nearly half of respondents (48%) identified accelerated digital transformation as a trend likely to have a substantial impact on their organizations in 2026.
Concern about geopolitical tensions has risen sharply, with 39% of respondents naming it as a top issue—a jump of 20 percentage points from the prior year.

The Deloitte 2026 Life Sciences Outlook Survey included 280 C-suite executives from biopharma and medtech companies across the United States, Europe (France, Germany, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom), and Asia (China and Japan).
90% of biopharma leaders in surveyed European and Asian countries report 'positive' or 'cautiously positive' expectations for 2026.
83% of biopharma leaders in surveyed European and Asian countries predict steady or strong revenue growth for 2026.
56% of US-based biopharma leaders express a positive or cautiously positive outlook for 2026, while 27% remain negative or uncertain.
71% of US biopharma respondents anticipate revenue gains, but 18% foresee a decline.
A US medtech supply chain executive noted a need to automate processes for customers due to insufficient phlebotomists, lab managers, and people capacity.
market_data_points: 280 C-suite executives from biopharma and medtech companies were surveyed between August and September 2025.
48% of respondents identified accelerated digital transformation as a substantial impact trend for 2026, a statistically significant increase compared with 2025.

38% of respondents identified inflation, broader economic pressures, and supply chain risks as factors likely to shape organizational strategies in 2026.
32% of respondents cited evolving customer needs and preferences as a top trend for 2026.
51% of non-US respondents pointed to national regulatory changes expected to shape organizational strategy in 2026.

Medtech executives anticipate 81% revenue growth, comparable to biopharma peers outside the US at 83%.

sources.title: Life Sciences & Health - Your 2026 funding roadmap
key_facts: Cardiovascular diseases cause 1.7 million deaths annually in the EU.
Cardiovascular diseases cost the EU €282 billion annually.
The EU medical devices sector employs nearly one million people.
The EU medical devices sector is worth €170 billion.
Proposed EU medical device regulatory reforms are projected to deliver €3.3 billion in yearly savings.
The EIC Pathfinder program funds early-stage, high-risk research at TRL 1-3 with 100% funding rate and a maximum grant of €4 million.
The EIC Transition program supports maturation of breakthrough technologies at TRL 4-5 with 100% funding rate and a maximum grant of €2.5 million.
The EIC Accelerator provides up to €2.5 million in grants plus €1-10 million in equity for SMEs at TRL 6-8 with a maximum 70% funding rate.
The EIC STEP initiative provides €10-30 million in equity investment for deep-tech companies at TRL 8-9.
Horizon Europe Health funding supports research at TRL 3-9 with grants of €6-8 million and up to 70-100% funding rate.
The Eurostars program supports innovative SMEs with grants up to €500k at TRL 4-6 with a maximum 50% funding rate.

sources.title: 2026 Global health care outlook
key_facts: More than 80% of health system executives surveyed in Australia, Canada, Germany, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom reported a 'positive' or 'cautiously positive' outlook for their own organizations for 2026.
72% of non-US health system executives surveyed said they were upbeat about the health care industry overall for 2026.
20% of US respondents expressed a negative industry outlook for 2026, and 33% expressed uncertainty—up from 3% who expressed uncertainty a year ago.
About 30% of surveyed health systems report operating generative AI at scale in select areas of their organizations.
Just 2% of surveyed health systems have deployed AI across their entire enterprise.
About 70% of non-US health system executives expect operating revenue and margins to increase in 2026.
Over 50% of non-US health system executives predict that operating costs will be flat or decline slightly in 2026.
Only 13% of respondents expect operating costs to increase 'significantly' in 2026.
64% of respondents said AI could reduce costs by standardizing and automating workflows.
55% of respondents see savings potential from increased use of predictive analytics to optimize the workforce.
49% of respondents expect benefits from tech-enabled patient engagement and remote monitoring.
Nearly half (45%) of non-US health system executives cited care model transformation as a leading trend in 2026.
38% of non-US health system executives said their organizations would focus on preventive care and early detection in 2026.
Only 7% of US health system executives expect preventive care to be a major trend for their organizations in 2026.
More than 90% of health system executives said improving productivity would be a priority in 2026.
The World Health Organization projects a shortage of 4.5 million nurses by 2030.
In the United Kingdom, 40% of general practitioners expect to leave the profession within the next five years.
Nearly 40% of today's job skills may become outdated because of AI and automation, according to the World Economic Forum.
Deloitte Global surveyed 180 C-suite executives from large health systems in August and September 2025 for its annual global outlook survey.
Survey respondents were based in Australia, Canada, Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and the United States.
Ransomware and supply chain attacks are identified as major threats to health systems around the world.
Health system leaders across all six countries agreed that their 2026 strategies will be strongly influenced by financial pressures, workforce challenges, and cybersecurity risks.
market_data_points: 180 C-suite executives from large health systems were surveyed in August and September 2025 across six countries.
30% of surveyed health systems report operating generative AI at scale in select areas as of 2025.
2% of surveyed health systems have deployed AI across their entire enterprise as of 2025.
The WHO projects a shortage of 4.5 million nurses by 2030.
40% of UK general practitioners expect to leave the profession within the next five years.
70% of non-US health system executives expect operating revenue and margins to increase in 2026.
64% of respondents identified AI-driven workflow standardization and automation as a source of cost reduction in 2026.
49% of health system executives expect benefits from tech-enabled patient engagement and remote monitoring in 2026.
33% of US health system executives expressed uncertainty about the industry outlook for 2026, up from 3% a year ago.
20% of US respondents expressed a negative industry outlook for 2026.
trend_signals: Remote monitoring and tech-enabled patient engagement are identified as key cost-saving and care transformation strategies for 2026.
Shift of care to lower-cost settings such as neighborhood clinics, outpatient facilities, and at-home care via remote monitoring and virtual visits is an emerging priority.
Expansion of outpatient services and digital care offerings is expected to contribute to revenue growth in 2026.
Preventive care and early detection are prioritized by 38% of non-US health system executives for 2026.
AI-driven risk stratification based on genetics, environment, and lifestyle is emerging as a proactive health intervention tool.
Generative AI and agentic AI are on the horizon for health care but most executives do not expect major strategic impact from AI in 2026.
Cybersecurity, particularly ransomware and supply chain attacks, is an escalating threat to health systems globally.
Offshoring of IT and administrative tasks to regions like Eastern Europe is a growing efficiency strategy for health systems.
Workforce shortages and aging populations are creating sustained pressure on global health systems through at least 2030.
Care model transformation toward whole-health and outcomes-based approaches is a key strategic direction for 2026.
regulatory_mentions: US health system leaders cited ongoing uncertainties regarding tariffs, drug pricing, and regulatory changes as contributing to a more cautious outlook for 2026.
The United Kingdom does not allow the offshoring of patient-level data, restricting certain efficiency strategies.
The fee-for-service model used predominantly in US private insurance incentivizes volume over value, emphasizing treatment over prevention.

sources.title: Pharmaceutical and life sciences: US Deals 2026 outlook
key_facts: The pharmaceutical sector enters 2026 with confidence and ample capital to deploy following a strong second half of 2025 defined by precision-driven biopharma M&A.
Dealmakers are prioritizing disciplined deployment of capital and meticulous portfolio-shaping to secure high-quality innovation and scarce assets.
Financial and strategic interest will continue to prioritize therapeutic areas including cardiometabolic, CNS, oncology, and immunology.
Truly differentiated clinical profiles continue to command elevated premiums with competitive processes producing outsized pricing for assets with meaningful patient benefits.
There has been a preference more recently for biopharma M&A in the $5B to $15B range.

China-to-the-West licensing and co-development programs are now a core vector in corporate and business development strategies as Chinese biotechs move efficiently through trials and scale manufacturing rapidly.
Private equity and structured financing are now mainstream tools to bridge the gap from late-stage development to commercialization via royalties, options, and minority interests.
Predictive models are sharpening the probability of technical and regulatory success (PTRS), safety, and value forecasts, compressing decision cycles.
The sector is increasingly shaped by tech-enabled, empowered consumers and patients who expect a seamless, end-to-end health experience.
Medtech deals are reported separately from pharmaceutical and life sciences deals by PwC.
market_data_points: Biopharma M&A preference has been concentrated in the $5B to $15B deal range in recent periods.
Global pharmaceutical revenue faces loss-of-exclusivity (LOE) headwinds ramping up over the next four years.
Activity in 2025 was skewed toward targeted and asset-centric transactions that filled pipeline gaps.
LOE pressures are described as mounting and becoming more pronounced over the next few years.
Interest rates are generally expected to be lower in 2026 relative to 2025.
trend_signals: Precision-led growth and asset-centric M&A transactions are expected to continue in 2026.
Larger-scale M&A may be pursued as LOE headwinds intensify and companies seek definitive therapeutic area strength coupled with IP runway.
Cross-border collaboration, particularly China-to-West licensing and co-development, is deepening and expected to increase in 2026.
AI is being embedded across diligence and post-close value-creation programs as a differentiator for leading dealmakers.
Capital structures are evolving toward alternatives including minority stakes, royalties, and staged options.
Biotech IPO listings and structured exits are expected to improve with better financing and funding environment in 2026.
Integration of diligence, regulatory planning, and manufacturing from the outset is identified as a key competitive differentiator.
Private equity is expected to remain active in pharma tech and pharma services sectors in 2026.
competitive_mentions: Western pharma companies are using structured licenses, regional development and commercialization rights, and financial tools to access Chinese biotech innovation.
Chinese biotechs are moving efficiently through trials and scaling manufacturing rapidly, making them attractive co-development partners.
EPS-challenged innovators are increasingly using private equity and structured financing structures for runway and flexibility.
regulatory_mentions: Assets with clear regulatory paths and credible commercial ramps are commanding elevated acquisition premiums.
Tariffs, pricing, and geopolitical headwinds held back biopharma dealmaking for the first part of 2025 but have somewhat receded.
Government policies are becoming more predictable, enabling dealmakers to pivot from wait-and-see toward proactive growth.
IP, data security, and supply chain risks are being managed through clear governance, data-segmentation protocols, and parallel manufacturing strategies in cross-border deals.
Regulatory planning integrated from the outset of deals is identified as translating clinical catalysts into faster approvals.
